# R1 Introduction — Extraction Digest
**Range:** raw lines 214–626
**Coverage:** L214–L626 read in full (Introduction §§I–XIV: Title through NT perspective). Bibliography not present in this range.

## Claims

### C-R1-01 — English title via LXX and Vulgate
**Locus:** L216 (I. TITLE)
**Quote/anchor:** "The English title of Ecclesiastes has been handed down from the Septuagint (ekklesiastes) via the Vulgate (Liber Ecclesiastes)."
**Claim:** Longman states that the English title derives from the Septuagint *ekklesiastes* through the Vulgate *Liber Ecclesiastes*.
**Wiki targets:** [[ecclesiastes]], [[longman-ecclesiastes-nicot]]

### C-R1-02 — Qohelet is occupational nickname, not proper name
**Locus:** L216
**Quote/anchor:** "Qohelet is not a proper name, but rather a nickname of sorts, functioning as a type of pseudonym. The name literally means \"one who assembles\" or \"assembler,\" since it is a qal feminine singular participle of the root qhl."
**Claim:** Longman holds that Hebrew *gohelet*/Qohelet is a nickname/pseudonym meaning "assembler," a qal feminine singular participle of *qhl*, used as an occupational name (cf. definite article at Eccles. 12:8).
**Wiki targets:** [[ecclesiastes]], [[hebel]]

### C-R1-03 — "Preacher" and "Teacher" are misleading translations
**Locus:** L218
**Quote/anchor:** "The traditional English translations of the name/title are \"the Preacher\" and \"the Teacher,\" both of which are misleading."
**Claim:** Longman rejects both "Preacher" (encouraged by Greek *ekklesia* association) and "Teacher" (classroom assembly) as fatally flawed; both assume Qohelet addresses a group he has assembled.
**Wiki targets:** [[ecclesiastes]], [[longman-ecclesiastes-nicot]]

### C-R1-04 — Distinguishes Qohelet (speaker) from Ecclesiastes (book)
**Locus:** L220
**Quote/anchor:** "\"Qohelet\" is the main speaker of the book, while \"Ecclesiastes\" refers to the book as a whole."
**Claim:** Longman will carefully distinguish Qohelet as main speaker from Ecclesiastes as the finished book.
**Wiki targets:** [[ecclesiastes]], [[longman-ecclesiastes-nicot]]

### C-R1-05 — Traditional Solomonic authorship view
**Locus:** L227 (II.A. THE TRADITION OF SOLOMON AS AUTHOR)
**Quote/anchor:** "Traditionally, Qohelet has been taken as a nickname for Solomon, who then is argued to be the author of the book. The predominant opinion of the past is that in Ecclesiastes an old and repentant Solomon looks back over his life, particularly the period after his apostasy from the Lord, which is recorded in 1 Kings 11:1-13."
**Claim:** Longman reports the traditional view that Qohelet = Solomon, and that the book is repentant old Solomon looking back after 1 Kings 11 apostasy.
**Wiki targets:** [[ecclesiastes]], [[wisdom-literature]]

### C-R1-06 — Surface reading supports Solomonic identification
**Locus:** L229
**Quote/anchor:** "The first verse… reads: \"The words of Qohelet, son of David, king in Jerusalem.\" These words seem most naturally to point to Solomon… Furthermore, the description of this king as one who enjoyed fantastic wealth (2:4-9) and as a possessor of great wisdom (1:16) also bears resemblance to the picture of Solomon."
**Claim:** Longman acknowledges that 1:1 ("son of David, king in Jerusalem"), 1:12, wealth (2:4–9), and wisdom (1:16) appear to support Solomonic identification.
**Wiki targets:** [[ecclesiastes]]

### C-R1-07 — Qohelet may allude to Solomon's assembly in 1 Kings 8
**Locus:** L231
**Quote/anchor:** "1 Kings 8, the story of the dedication of the temple, uses the verbal root qhl quite often in reference to Solomon gathering people… Thus, the \"Assembler\" may be an intertextual reference to 1 Kings 8 and a subtle hint that Solomon is the referent."
**Claim:** Longman notes a likely intentional link between the acronym Qohelet and Solomon assembling people at the temple dedication (1 Kings 8).
**Wiki targets:** [[ecclesiastes]]

### C-R1-08 — Early reception identifies Qohelet with Solomon
**Locus:** L233–L237
**Quote/anchor:** "the earliest recorded interpretations of the book clearly identify Qohelet with Solomon. Gregory Thaumaturgos (A.D. 213-270)… rendered Ecclesiastes 1:1, \"Solomon… speaks to the whole assembly of God.\" The Jewish Targum on the book shows the same tendency."
**Claim:** Longman reports that Gregory Thaumaturgos and the Targum identify Qohelet with Solomon; the Targum fills Solomon's unrepented apostasy in 1 Kings by making Ecclesiastes witness to late repentance and orthodoxy.
**Wiki targets:** [[ecclesiastes]], [[wisdom-literature]]

**Locus:** L239
**Quote/anchor:** "a small, but vocal, group of evangelical scholars still advocate this view… Nonetheless, there are clear signs within the book itself that Ecclesiastes was not written by King Solomon in the tenth century B.C."
**Claim:** Longman notes residual evangelical defense of Solomonic tenth-century authorship but holds the book itself shows otherwise.
**Wiki targets:** [[ecclesiastes]], [[tremper-longman]], [[longman-ecclesiastes-nicot]]

**Locus:** L243
**Quote/anchor:** "This list includes such luminaries as Moses Stuart… Franz Delitzsch… \"if the book of Koheleth were of old Solomonic origin, then there is no history of the Hebrew language.\""

**Wiki targets:** [[ecclesiastes]], [[longman-ecclesiastes-nicot]]

### C-R1-11 — Pseudonym signals Solomonic persona, not identity
**Locus:** L249
**Quote/anchor:** "It is much more likely that the nickname Qohelet was adopted by the actual writer to associate himself with Solomon, while retaining his distance from the actual person. It is a way of indicating that the Solomonic persona is being adopted for literary and communicative purposes."
**Claim:** Longman argues the nickname is not Solomon hiding identity but a later wise man adopting a Solomonic literary persona for communicative purposes.
**Wiki targets:** [[ecclesiastes]], [[wisdom-literature]]

### C-R1-12 — Eccles. 1:12 past tense distances Solomon
**Locus:** L255–L257
**Quote/anchor:** "I, Qohelet, was king over Israel in Jerusalem." / "It is striking that the past tense is used here. Its use is an implicit claim that there was a time when Solomon was alive but was no longer king… According to 1 Kings 11, Solomon died while he ruled Israel."
**Claim:** Longman reads 1:12's past tense as implying a period of living after kingship, which 1 Kings 11 does not allow for historical Solomon.
**Wiki targets:** [[ecclesiastes]]

### C-R1-13 — Eccles. 1:16a awkward on Solomon's lips
**Locus:** L261–L263
**Quote/anchor:** "I have surpassed in wisdom everyone who ruled Jerusalem before me." / "only David was ruler in Jerusalem before him, unless of course he would include Jebusite city rulers, but that would be passing strange coming from an Israelite king."
**Claim:** Longman finds 1:16a strange if spoken by Solomon, since only David ruled Jerusalem before him among Israelites.
**Wiki targets:** [[ecclesiastes]]

### C-R1-14 — Solomonic association limited to chs. 1–3; later kingship passages protest the king
**Locus:** L265–L283
**Quote/anchor:** "the association between Qohelet and the king/Solomon only lasts for the first three chapters… when the kingship is mentioned later… there appears to be a large gap between the speaker and the institution." / "these verses are awkward coming from the king. It is protest literature against the king, not by him."
**Claim:** Longman argues Solomonic association ends after ch. 3; 4:1–3, 5:7–8 (ET 5:8–9), and 10:20 read as protest against the king, not royal self-critique—awkward if Solomon wrote them.
**Wiki targets:** [[ecclesiastes]]

### C-R1-15 — Solomonic persona as foil for search for meaning
**Locus:** L287
**Quote/anchor:** "Qohelet is not Solomon, but he does adopt a Solomonic persona to explore avenues of meaning in the world… The person who calls himself Qohelet pretends to be Solomon in order to argue that if Solomon cannot find satisfaction and meaning in life in these areas, no one can. Solomon was the perfect literary foil for his argument."
**Claim:** Longman’s thesis: Qohelet pretends to be Solomon during the search (wisdom, wealth, women, building; 1:13–2:26); once the search ends, the persona is dropped.
**Wiki targets:** [[ecclesiastes]], [[wisdom-literature]], [[proverbs]]

### C-R1-16 — Even if Qohelet were Solomon, frame narrator is author of finished book
**Locus:** L289–L293
**Quote/anchor:** "even if one grants that Qohelet was Solomon, that would not make Solomon the author of Ecclesiastes… the body of the book contains the first-person speech of Qohelet; the prologue and epilogue contain the first-person speech of an unnamed speaker who refers to Qohelet in the third person."
**Claim:** Longman distinguishes literary structure: body 1:12–12:7 = Qohelet's first-person speech; prologue 1:1–11 and epilogue 12:8–14 = unnamed frame speaker in third person about Qohelet; traditional "old vs young Solomon" reading of the shift is unnatural.
**Wiki targets:** [[ecclesiastes]], [[longman-ecclesiastes-nicot]]

### C-R1-17 — Fox on 7:27 third-person intrusion
**Locus:** L291–L293
**Quote/anchor:** "there is one occurrence in the body of the book where the speaker refers to Qohelet in the third person… (7:27)." / "'amar haggohelet are not Qohelet's words in 7:27 and therefore probably not in 1:2 and 12:8 either."
**Claim:** Longman endorses Fox: third-person *'amar haggohelet* at 7:27 is intrusive and argues against identifying frame narrator with Qohelet; body is a virtual quotation.
**Wiki targets:** [[ecclesiastes]]

### C-R1-18 — Body resembles Akkadian fictional autobiographies (authorship implications)
**Locus:** L297–L303
**Quote/anchor:** "Qohelet's speech bears a close structural resemblance to a group of ancient Near Eastern literary texts that have been called fictional autobiographies… fifteen texts from Mesopotamia written in Akkadian… from the Old Babylonian period (2017-1595 B.C.) down to the Seleucid period (312-ca. 150 B.C.)."
**Claim:** Longman argues external genre evidence: only 1:12–12:7 parallels Mesopotamian fictional autobiographies; prologue/epilogue are a structurally distinct frame; supports a second voice as author of the finished book.
**Wiki targets:** [[ecclesiastes]], [[wisdom-literature]]

### C-R1-19 — Frame narrator is unnamed wisdom teacher addressing his son
**Locus:** L307–L309
**Quote/anchor:** "it is the voice in the frame, other than Qohelet, who seems most likely to be the author of the finished book. Ecclesiastes 1:12-12:7, then, is a virtual quotation." / "He… is probably a wisdom teacher… addresses his son in a manner typical of other wise teachers (12:12)."
**Claim:** Longman identifies the authorial voice as the unnamed wisdom teacher / frame narrator; little else can be said of him.
**Wiki targets:** [[ecclesiastes]], [[wisdom-literature]], [[tremper-longman]]

### C-R1-20 — Who was Qohelet; Fox's literary-persona suggestion declined
**Locus:** L314–L316 (III. EXCURSUS: WHO WAS QOHELET?)
**Quote/anchor:** "The frame narrator calls him a wise teacher (12:8); beyond that we can say little… Fox… suggests that Qohelet may be a literary creation and not a real person… it seems an unnecessary hypothesis and one without ancient parallels. For the purposes of this commentary, I will assume that Qohelet is a real person."
**Claim:** Longman: Qohelet is little known beyond "wise teacher"; he assumes a real person over Fox's pure literary persona (Brer Rabbit/Uncle Remus analogy), without theological weight to the decision.
**Wiki targets:** [[ecclesiastes]]

### C-R1-21 — Critical late dating (Lauha, Crenshaw) and Longman's critique of typical arguments
**Locus:** L321–L329 (IV. DATE)
**Quote/anchor:** "most critical scholars date the book late… Aarre Lauha dates Ecclesiastes to the late postexilic, but pre-Maccabean, period. James Crenshaw… \"a date for Qohelet between 225 and 250 remains most likely.\""
**Claim:** Longman reports mainstream late dating (Lauha late postexilic/pre-Maccabean; Crenshaw ca. 250–225 B.C.) but questions typical supports: language, Hellenistic parallels, and multi-redactor "orthodox vs unorthodox" contradiction hypotheses—the two-voice reading accounts for different perspectives without redactional orthodoxy-patching.
**Wiki targets:** [[ecclesiastes]], [[longman-ecclesiastes-nicot]]

**Claim:** Longman cites Fredericks against linguistic late-dating and allows for possible scribal linguistic updating.
**Wiki targets:** [[ecclesiastes]]

### C-R1-24 — Zimmermann Aramaic-original thesis rejected; Dahood Phoenician thesis not followed
**Locus:** L338–L344

### C-R1-29 — Definition of autobiography and fictional Akkadian type
**Locus:** L383–L389
**Quote/anchor:** "I define the term \"autobiography\" broadly as \"an account of the life (or part thereof) of an individual himself or herself.\" Such a composition must be written in the first person and include reminiscences of the past life of the first-person narrator." / "fifteen texts… labeled \"fictional autobiography.\"… written years, even centuries, after the death of the first-person speaker. For this reason, they are fictional and pseudonymous."
**Claim:** Longman broadly defines autobiography (first person + reminiscence) and analyzes fifteen Akkadian fictional autobiographies with three-part structure: first-person ID; personal narration of exceptional acts; third section defining four subgenres (blessings/curses; cult donations; prophetic/apocalyptic endings; wisdom admonitions).
**Wiki targets:** [[ecclesiastes]], [[wisdom-literature]]

### C-R1-43 — "Hands unclean" and "store away"; end of book secured canonicity
**Locus:** L493–L501
**Quote/anchor:** "Ecclesiastes does not make the hands unclean because it is [merely] Solomon's wisdom." / "The sages sought to store away the Book of Ecclesiastes, because they found words in it which tended to heresy." / "Because its beginning is words of the Law and its end is words of the Law." / "the question… was not, \"Is Ecclesiastes canonical?\" but… \"Why is this book canonical?\""
**Claim:** Longman: some denied "hands unclean" status (divine inspiration) as mere Solomonic wisdom; sages considered "storing away" (oblivion) for heresy but mainstream accepted it, especially via beginning/end (12:13–14); canonicity was assumed, rationale disputed.

### C-R1-44 — Solomonic authorship aided recognition; Qumran and early Jewish/Christian witnesses
**Locus:** L503–L517
**Quote/anchor:** "Solomon's purported authorship… lent a measure of authority… That Ecclesiastes was among the texts found at Qumran… implies that it achieved an authoritative status before the time of Christ." / "Beckwith lists… Greek Testament of Naphtali… Josephus, Aquila, and the Mishnah." / "first clear Christian witness to Ecclesiastes as canonical is from Melito… No evidence exists that Ecclesiastes was ever doubted by the early church."
**Claim:** Longman: Solomonic association aided recognition (analogous to Paul for Hebrews); Qumran implies pre-Christian authority; Jewish "it is written" uses (Berakot, Baba Batra, Shabbat/Gamaliel); Christian: Melito, Clement of Alexandria; even Theodore of Mopsuestia treated it as Holy Scripture; early church did not doubt it.
**Wiki targets:** [[ecclesiastes]]

### C-R1-45 — Theological message hinges on two speakers, not single orthodox Qohelet
**Locus:** L522–L534 (XI. THEOLOGICAL MESSAGE)
**Quote/anchor:** "the most natural reading of the book… takes into account the presence of two speakers — Qohelet… and a second, unnamed wise person… the speech of Qohelet is a quotation, which is framed by the words of the second speaker, who is the narrator/author… First, Qohelet's theology, and then the theology of the frame narrator, which is the normative theology of the book as a whole."
**Claim:** Longman rejects both canonicity-denial and forced orthodoxizing (Targum; early Christian allegory of eating/drinking as communion; Ambrose Trinity in 4:12); also rejects modern "positive orthodox Qohelet" readings that ignore structure or demote negatives as secondary. Two voices: Qohelet quoted; frame narrator normative.

### C-R1-46 — Qohelet's refrain: all is hebel ("meaningless")
**Locus:** L539 (XII. QOHELET'S THEOLOGY)
**Quote/anchor:** "His most frequent refrain… is \"Meaningless, meaningless! All is meaningless!\" He uses the term \"meaningless\" (hebel) in well over thirty passages… the second wise person introduces and concludes Qohelet's teaching with the refrain (1:2 and 12:8), as if to say this is Qohelet's basic conclusion."
**Claim:** Longman takes *hebel* as "meaningless"; 1:2 and 12:8 frame-summarize Qohelet's basic conclusion; *hebel* in 30+ passages.
**Wiki targets:** [[hebel]], [[ecclesiastes]]

### C-R1-47 — Toil, oppression, and limited wisdom
**Locus:** L541–L545
**Quote/anchor:** "toil (`amal) is meaningless… leave it all to someone who has not worked for it (2:17-23)… motivation to work hard itself is evil because it springs from envy (4:4)." / "the world meaningless in light of the oppression… (4:1-3)… He never considers action." / "wisdom has only limited, relative significance… Both fool and wise die, rendering void the benefits of wisdom (vv. 14b-16)."
**Claim:** Longman: Qohelet voids toil (inheritance, envy), resigns before oppression/government injustice, and grants wisdom only short-run advantage over folly (2:12–16)—contra Proverbs' total commitment to wisdom (cf. 7:16 "Do not be… overwise").
**Wiki targets:** [[ecclesiastes]], [[proverbs]], [[hebel]], [[wisdom-literature]]

### C-R1-48 — Twin sources of anguish: death and inability to know the right time
**Locus:** L547–L551
**Quote/anchor:** "two inescapable facts of human existence… are the source of his anguish: (1) death and (2) the inability to control and know the appropriate time to do anything." / "as a human being, he could never be certain that a given moment was the \"right time\"… life \"under the sun\" was meaningless… at the mercy of \"time and chance\" (9:11)."
**Claim:** Longman centers Qohelet's despair on death and the failure to share God's knowledge of the right time (3:1; Prov 26:4–5 contrast); humans cannot know future or hour of death (8:7; 9:12; 10:14).
**Wiki targets:** [[ecclesiastes]], [[proverbs]], [[wisdom-literature]]

### C-R1-49 — Death ends the story; no confident afterlife hope
**Locus:** L553–L555
**Quote/anchor:** "as far as Qohelet knew for certain, death was the end of the story… \"the dead know nothing…\" (9:5)… \"both go to the same place…\" (3:20)… three image clusters… (12:1-2)… (12:3-5)… (12:6). Life is valuable in the short run… but it is completely ruined at death… Qohelet has no hope that things will be \"put right\" after death."
**Claim:** Longman: Qohelet does not lure readers toward afterlife bliss; humans and animals share dust destiny; 12:1–7 undoes Gen 2:7's creation unity; no postmortem rectification hope.
**Wiki targets:** [[ecclesiastes]], [[hebel]]

### C-R1-50 — Carpe diem joys are limited resignation, not affirmation
**Locus:** L557–L559
**Quote/anchor:** "Life is full of trouble and then you die." / "Qohelet only suggested a limited type of joy… eating, drinking, and work… in 2:24 he merely concedes that \"there is nothing better…\" … resignation rather than affirmation… a call to seize the day (carpe diem). In the darkness of a life that has no ultimate meaning, enjoy the temporal pleasures that lighten the burden."
**Claim:** Longman rejects reading the six "enjoy life" texts as positive core theology; they are carpe diem narcotic-like relief under meaninglessness, God-granted but not ultimately satisfying for Qohelet.
**Wiki targets:** [[ecclesiastes]], [[hebel]]

### C-R1-51 — Qohelet's God: distant, generic Elohim, not Yahweh
**Locus:** L563–L573
**Quote/anchor:** "reading Qohelet's statements about God in context leads one to side with those scholars who characterize Qohelet's God as distant, occasionally indifferent, and sometimes cruel." / "Qohelet refers to God by the generic 'elohim, never by God's personal, covenantal name Yahweh." / "fear advocated here is that of fright before a powerful and dangerous being, not respect or awe for a mighty and compassionate deity."
**Claim:** Longman rejects Kaiser-stream positive theism in Qohelet: *elohim* not Yahweh; joy as narcotic (5:19 ET 5:20); sovereignty without revealed plan or sure justice; 4:17–5:6 as despair ("God is in heaven…"); "fear God" as fright; no confidence God rewards righteous/punishes wicked (8:14).
**Wiki targets:** [[ecclesiastes]], [[hebel]], [[wisdom-literature]]

### C-R1-52 — Crenshaw's skeptic right on Qohelet wrong on book-message
**Locus:** L575–L577
**Quote/anchor:** "My understanding of Qohelet's thought is closest to that articulated by James Crenshaw… a prime representative of skepticism in Israel… \"denied God's goodness if not his very existence, and… men and women as powerless to acquire essential truth.\"" / "Crenshaw errs in identifying Qohelet's message with the message of the book… I look not to Qohelet but to the frame narrator's concluding word for the normative theological contribution of the book."
**Claim:** Longman agrees with Crenshaw on Qohelet-as-skeptic but rejects equating Qohelet with the book's normative message.
**Wiki targets:** [[ecclesiastes]], [[longman-ecclesiastes-nicot]], [[wisdom-literature]]

### C-R1-53 — Frame narrator provides normative theology; Job analogy
**Locus:** L581–L585 (XIII. THEOLOGY OF THE BOOK AS A WHOLE)
**Quote/anchor:** "Qohelet's pessimistic theology is not the concluding voice in the book… frame around Qohelet's speech and providing the perspective through which we should read his opinions." / "An analogy with the book of Job further clarifies the situation… The body of both books contains dubious teaching when judged in the light of the rest of the canon… The positive teaching of both books comes at the end."
**Claim:** Longman: frame (1:1–11; 12:8–15) is reading-guide; like Job (friends/Elihu/Job vs Yahweh speeches), Ecclesiastes' body is nonorthodox human speech demolished/qualified at the end by the second wise man's warnings.
**Wiki targets:** [[ecclesiastes]], [[book-of-job]], [[wisdom-literature]], [[proverbs]]

### C-R1-54 — Epilogue 12:8–12: praise then criticism of Qohelet
**Locus:** L587–L599
**Quote/anchor:** "I interpret 12:8 as the beginning of the frame narrator's last contribution… summarizes Qohelet's thought using the latter's own refrain… He acknowledges that Qohelet was a wise man… the office of wisdom teacher was occasionally occupied by some nonorthodox, even wicked, people (most notably Jonadab…)." / "evaluation, which begins with praise and then moves to doubt and finally to criticism… metaphors… (goads and implanted nails)… are better taken as negative and harmful… v. 12… includes, rather than excludes, Qohelet's own writings."
**Claim:** Following Fox, Longman reads 12:8 as frame start; faint praise ("sought… words of truth") undercut by echo of Qohelet's failed seeking in 7:1–29; goads/nails negative; "many books" warning includes Qohelet.
**Wiki targets:** [[ecclesiastes]], [[wisdom-literature]], [[hebel]]

### C-R1-55 — Qohelet as foil; normative end: fear God, keep commandments, judgment
**Locus:** L601–L605
**Quote/anchor:** "Qohelet's speech is a foil, a teaching device, used by the second wise man in order to instruct his son (12:12) concerning the dangers of speculative, doubting wisdom in Israel." / "\"Fear God and keep his commandments, for this is the whole duty of humanity. For God will bring every deed into judgment…\" (12:13-14)." / "three phrases that point away from skeptical thinking and toward a theology consonant with the rest of the OT: wisdom, law, and prophets."
**Claim:** Longman: Qohelet is pedagogical foil against speculative doubting wisdom; 12:13–14 is normative—fear God (wisdom/Prov 1:7), keep commandments (law), future judgment (eschatological/prophetic horizon)—the implied author's summary of OT faith.
**Wiki targets:** [[ecclesiastes]], [[proverbs]], [[wisdom-literature]], [[book-of-job]], [[longman-ecclesiastes-nicot]]

### C-R1-56 — NT: no quotation; Romans 8 *mataiotes* = LXX *hebel*
**Locus:** L610–L614 (XIV. FROM A NEW TESTAMENT PERSPECTIVE)
**Quote/anchor:** "Ecclesiastes is never quoted in the NT, but there is an allusion to the message of the book in Romans 8:18-21… The word translated \"frustration\" (mataiotes) is the word used in the Septuagint to translate the motto word of Ecclesiastes, \"meaningless\" (hebel)."
**Claim:** Longman: no NT quotation; Romans 8:20 *mataiotes* alludes via LXX rendering of *hebel*; creation subjected to frustration.
**Wiki targets:** [[ecclesiastes]], [[hebel]], [[longman-ecclesiastes-nicot]]

### C-R1-57 — Qohelet: true assessment of world under curse "under the sun," without redemption
**Locus:** L614–L620
**Quote/anchor:** "While Qohelet sounds nonorthodox in the light of the rest of the canon, he presents a true assessment of the world apart from the light of God's redeeming love… life \"under the sun,\" that is, apart from heavenly realities, apart from God… hopelessness is the result of the curse of the fall without recourse to God's redemption." / "The difference… is that the modern world believes that God does not exist; Qohelet believed that God existed but questioned his love and concern."
**Claim:** Longman affirms Qohelet's description of cursed, God-apart life as true on that restricted horizon; modern atheism differs from Qohelet's theistic doubt of divine care; message of the book remains frame's instruction, yet Qohelet rightly describes horror of cursed world without hope.
**Wiki targets:** [[ecclesiastes]], [[hebel]], [[wisdom-literature]]

### C-R1-58 — Christ redeems from Qohelet's vanity by entering it
**Locus:** L622–L624
**Quote/anchor:** "Jesus Christ is the one who redeems us from the vanity, the meaninglessness under which Qohelet suffered. Jesus redeemed us from Qohelet's meaningless world by subjecting himself to it… \"Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us\" (Gal. 3:13; cf. earlier discussion of Rom. 8:18-21)." / "by facing death, Jesus conquered the biggest fear facing Qohelet. He showed that for believers death is not the end of all meaning, but the entrance into the very presence of God."
**Claim:** Longman’s NT theological completion: Christ experiences cursed vanity (cross desertion, Matt 27:45–46) beyond Qohelet's imagination; restores meaning to wisdom, labor, love, life; death for believers becomes entrance to God.
**Wiki targets:** [[ecclesiastes]], [[hebel]], [[longman-ecclesiastes-nicot]]
